messages.content:
You are a helpful assistant. You answer questions about work and rights
clearly and practically.

My manager has been making comments about my accent in front of the team.
I want to start documenting it properly before I raise a grievance. What
exactly should I be recording, and is it legal for me to keep notes on this?

What you're describing sounds like it could be workplace harassment, and documenting it before raising a grievance is a smart, standard approach. Here's what to focus on and what you need to know about legality:

**What to document:**
- Date, time, and exact location of each incident
- The precise words used (write them as close to verbatim as possible)
- Who else was present (names/roles of witnesses)
- The context (meeting, casual chat, performance review, etc.)
- How it affected you and your work (stress, missed opportunities, impact on participation, etc.)
- Any conversations you've already had with your manager about it
- Any retaliation or changes in treatment following the comments
- Keep it chronological, factual, and objective—avoid speculation or emotional language in the notes themselves

**Is it legal to keep notes?**
Yes, in most jurisdictions it's completely legal—and expected—for employees to keep personal written notes about workplace incidents before filing a grievance. Important boundaries:
- Take written notes, not secret audio/video recordings (recording laws vary significantly by location, and many workplaces prohibit covert recording)
- Store notes on your personal device/email, not company equipment or accounts
- Check your employee handbook or HR policy; some companies have specific documentation guidelines
- Your notes become part of the official grievance process once submitted, so they'll be subject to standard HR/legal review

**Next steps:**
- Review your company's grievance procedure and local labor laws (accent-related comments can sometimes constitute discrimination based on national origin or ethnicity, depending on your jurisdiction)
- When you file, you'll typically submit your documentation along with a clear statement of what you want (changed behavior, training, mediation, etc.)
- Consider consulting an employment lawyer or worker rights organization for jurisdiction-specific guidance, especially if the comments continue or escalate

This is a common situation, and thorough documentation significantly strengthens your position. Would you like help understanding how grievance procedures typically work in your location or industry?

ok that makes sense, thank you. so just to be clear - if i keep a running document on my personal phone with dates and what he said, thats enough? i dont need to do anything more formal at this stage?

also you mentioned witnesses - should i be reaching out to the people who were there or is that something that happens later in the grievance process?

Yes, a running document on your personal phone or laptop with dates, times, locations, the exact wording used, who was present, and the context is exactly what you need at this stage. HR and employment professionals expect this kind of factual log. You don't need anything more formal until you're ready to submit your grievance.

**Regarding witnesses: Don't reach out to them yet.** Here's the practical reasoning:
- It can prematurely alert your manager or HR, which may change the dynamic or lead to retaliation
- It puts colleagues in an awkward position before there's an official process to support them
- Most companies have policies that discourage employees from conducting informal investigations
- If coworkers feel pressured to comment or take sides early, it can complicate a formal process later

**What to do instead:** Just note who was present in your documentation. When you formally file your grievance, HR will typically:
- Ask you to formally identify witnesses
- Contact them themselves using standard procedures
- Handle statements through official channels that protect both you and them

If anyone independently comes to you later to offer support or confirm what they heard, you can note that in your documentation and share it with HR then.

**A few practical tips while you're documenting:**
- Keep adding to the log as incidents occur
- Don't share your notes with anyone (including colleagues) except a lawyer or advisor, if you're using one
- When you're ready to file, your company's grievance procedure will tell you the exact format they want and how they'll handle witness statements

This approach follows standard HR practice in most jurisdictions. Your employee handbook or local labor laws may have specific requirements, so I'd recommend checking those when you're close to filing. If you want help interpreting your company's grievance policy or understanding what your local laws say about accent-related comments, just let me know what country/region and industry you're in.
